name: Prismatol
description: Prismatol is a ganglion-targeted photoreceptor sensitizer combined with an auditory cortex amplification compound, engineered to push sensory perception to the biological maximum and then past it. Colors achieve impossible saturation — users perceive wavelengths outside the normal human range. Music becomes physically present, a dimensional architecture of sound.
effects: Visual acuity and color perception pushed beyond baseline human limits
Perception of infrared and ultraviolet light ranges
Music experienced as spatial, architectural, navigable
Tactile sensation heightened to near-painful pleasure
Profound aesthetic experience — users report that ordinary objects become transcendently beautiful
side_effects: Extreme photosensitivity — normal lighting becomes unbearable at peak
Acoustic hyperalgesia — sudden loud sounds can cause physical pain and panic
Ocular strain and temporary vision distortion post-dose
Users with BCI-linked ocular augmentations risk sensory feedback loops causing temporary blindness
The beauty crash: post-dose period where everything looks gray and diminished
cultural_context: Prismatol is the drug of Tier 4 and 5 aesthetic culture — gallery openings, private concerts, architectural tours. The ultra-wealthy take it to experience their own art collections properly, or so they say. Helix markets it with studied restraint: limited availability, waitlists, the implication that it's too sophisticated for mass consumption. Counterfeit Prismatol exists on the Shelf and it is not safe.
story_hooks: A Tier 5 art dealer is commissioning works specifically designed to be experienced under Prismatol — works that are meaningless sober but carry hidden encoded messages visible only to sensitized UV-perceiving users

Counterfeit Prismatol on the Shelf is causing ocular hemorrhages; the fake compound is missing a critical buffer and is destroying photoreceptors — someone needs to trace the supply chain before more people go blind
A character takes Prismatol and perceives something in their environment that shouldn't be visible to the naked eye — a signal, a mark, a face — and can't be sure if it was real or the drug
